note_tweet.text:
I agree with @FerroTV ... the Fed has a bunch of post-GFC structures in place  they would like to get rid of, or at least radically change. These are the FOMC statement, the press conference, the dot plot and the summary of economic projections.

In particular, the press conference was designed for the chairman to provide forward guidance, or tell everybody what's coming next.

Warsh does not believe in forward guidance, and I agree with him. 

I've argued that forward guidance has caused as much damage, if not more, than the problems it has solved.

For instance, it kept the Fed from hiking rates in 2021/early 2022 because they were telling us inflation was "transitory." That was a big mistake

So he'd be better off canceling the presser, but the institutional prerogative tells them not to, so every press conference is a useless mess  as he has no forward guidance to offer, no one knows what to ask him if he's not giving forward guidance.

urls.description: We investigate the conditions under which black hole fragmentation, the splitting of a black hole into two or multiple smaller ones, may occur via an unspecified dynamics, which would have the topology of a pair-of-pants. We employ kinematical and entropical consideration on time-sliced quasistatic black hole configurations to check under what conditions the pants dynamics is permitted. In classical general relativity, the Bekenstein-Hawking area law forbids such processes for Schwarzschild black holes. For spinning Kerr black holes, purely kinematic analyses impose constraints that prevent fragmentation, even in regimes where entropy considerations might allow it, except possibly in near-extremal cases. We then hunt for scenarios where black holes can wear pants: from the well-known Gregory-Laflamme instability in higher dimensions, to the potential effect of superradiant instabilities in nonaxisymmetric radiation trapping, to finally gravitational models that modify the relations bet

article.plain_text:
Newer models require less prompting than most of us still do.
For Opus 5.5, try giving Claude a single prompt with a clear goal of what you want to do and how Claude should verify it has achieved it, and let Claude work on it. Start with /effort medium and adjust as needed. 
 
If you don't know yet what you're trying to do, ask Claude to interview you until it could write a spec. Then start a new session and use that spec to build what you want.
Claude will stop on its own when it believes it's done. 
If it can execute something that checks in terms of pass/fail or a number to beat, with reports in a way it can read, Claude can keep going without you having to watch. 
For long background tasks, you can use /goal to specify a condition that a separate model to check after every turn. 
Recent versions of Claude Code have also adopted auto mode as the default starting mode for interactive terminal sessions. In that mode, a classifier analyzes Claude's actions rather than relying on the usual permission prompts. This is not a guarantee of safe behavior - neither is blindly approving every prompt. When Claude reports back, ask it to show you the command and output or a screenshot.
For models like Claude Opus 5 and Claude Fable 5, over 80% of the Claude Code system prompt was removed with no measurable degradation of its coding evals. 
When a new model like Opus 5.5 comes out, you can do the same experiment with your own instructions: remove some, then add back only those that the model misses. The /doctor prompt-audit command flags those written for older models.
 
Another area to reduce your own work is subagents. 
Claude delegates to them on its own, so you rarely need to ask. Ask only for substantial, standalone work like long audits or migrations, which Opus 5.5 can split across parallel subagents. For small jobs, subagents multiply cost and latency. Subagents can parallelize work or provide a second opinion, but they don't, by default, make things smarter. 
For agents you build, a single agent with skills can outperform a subagent design on quality, often at lower cost and latency from what I’ve seen.
Use Claude cloud sessions when you want to shut your laptop. Start one from claude.ai/code, the Claude app or via claude --cloud. Cloud sessions run in a separate VM with a fresh clone of your repo, so be sure to push any commits before you start. Check in from your phone, address any questions the session posed, then review the diff and open the PR. Keep a session local if the task requires resources that are only available on your machine.
Parallel sessions only pay off once a single session can finish without you. If you have Projects in Claude Code, I think you'd find them very useful. Without a project, you are the manager of multiple sessions and must track what each session is doing, and which ones have completed. 
 
A project is one long-running chat that does most of the project management for you: as issues and jobs come up, paste them in, and Claude creates a separate thread (usually a cloud session) for each and runs them in parallel. You provide instructions once, and they are applied to all new threads. And the Overview shows which tasks have completed, which PRs are ready and what's pending your input. 
Projects are in public beta on Pro and Max, so you may not have them yet, but hopefully soon!
Review still matters. On the Claude Code team, however, most of the reading has become automated: most changes are reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. You can use Code Review on Team and Enterprise plans or the lighter /code-review, which reviews your diff in a subagent that hasn't seen the conversation. You can also simply start a new session. If you do, give it the spec and tell it to ignore stylistic stuff.
Every few months, audit how you work to make sure you aren't building for how older models used to work.

The ideal Napoleonic charge - especially the French heavy cavalry's version - was less a wild gallop than a carefully built crescendo. Squadrons started at a walk, moved through the trot and canter, and only went full out in the last stretch so the horses stayed fresh and the ranks stayed locked together ("boot to boot," or charge en muraille "like a wall"). That tight wall of men and mounts was meant to hit with real shock, preferably against an enemy already shaken by guns or infantry.

British cavalry of this era often approached the same problem differently. They had fine horses and bold riders, and a single squadron could be formidable. Yet they had a well-known habit of prioritising speed over control - once they charged, they tended to keep going, scatter, and struggle to re-form. Wellington put it bluntly when he said he considered British cavalry inferior to the French from "want of order," adding that while one British squadron might match two French, larger formations generally favoured the French. In small numbers that dash could still win, but in larger masses the French usually held the edge because they kept better cohesion and were more reliable about holding reserves.

The basic sequence of the charge was much the same on both sides. What set the French practice apart was simply greater consistency in keeping large bodies under control from start to finish.

Sharing a new piece in Foreign Policy with the fantastic Ma Xiao from PKU, unpacking some of the local govt dynamics behind China's industrial policy, and why they make Beijing's efforts to rein in overcapacity so difficult!

(By the way Xiao has done, in my mind, some of the most insightful research on this topic… Add his work to your reading list if you have not already done so!)

The general idea: we tend to talk about “China’s industrial policy” as if it is coherent. Many already understand that local governments have their own incentives and that implementation differs. But how do they actually bargain, compete, improvise(!), and sometimes push much further than Beijing intended?

We start with two puzzles:

Beijing planned for 12,000 km of high-speed rail by 2020; China ended up with roughly 40,000 km.

Beijing's auto ambition was to have a small number of large SOEs and JVs. Instead, many of the real stars like Geely, BYD, Nio, etc. are private firms backed by local governments, often finding ways around regulatory restrictions with local help.

Our key argument: local governments are (opportunistic) policy entrepreneurs.

They have few formal ways to push their interests at the top, so they cultivate allies, bargain through ministries, back private firms, launch things first and seek approval later… and compete intensely for one scarce resource: top leadership attention!

That “attention economy” is key. Hence the focus on showcase projects. And hence, when it comes to stuff that looks good on camera, e.g., EVs, drones, robotics, etc., they pile in.

The fiscal angle has of course been discussed too, but is also key: Local governments still have every incentive to prop up firms, protect employment, avoid bankruptcies, etc., especially in places with few alternatives. The Shenzhens of China can afford to let a zombie EV firm fail; an already fiscally constrained city heavily dependent on one or two industries has very different options.

Then there is the cadre system. Officials get credit for launching a mega project, then often rotate elsewhere before the costs / waste / downside risks show up. The average tenure of provincial and city leaders is only about three and a half years, so achievements have to show up fast.

We then use this framework to explain why rebalancing toward consumption is so hard: consumption is slow-moving, difficult to measure as a local KPI, and hard to credit to a particular locality… and why reining in local debt is so difficult, since debt-led growth shows up before the consequences do.

Full article below:

China’s Overcapacity Has a Mind of Its Own
Beijing can’t rein in its own industrial machine.

https://t.co/2GQBWVzqYO
